core_concepts: Chapter 1 The Uncomfortable Truth On a small plot of land in the monotonous countryside of central Europe, amid the warehouses of a former military barracks, a nexus of geographically concentrated evil would arise, de
It is the stuff of fairy tales and comic books: a hero marches headlong into the fiery jaws of hell to confront some great manifestation of evil
And for a brief time, there is hope
But this is not a story of hope
Witold Pilecki was already a war hero before he decided to sneak into Auschwitz
Then that whole Hitler thing happened, and before Poland could get both its boots on, the Nazis had already Blitzkrieged through half the country
Early on, the Soviets were actually far crueler than the Nazis
Pilecki fought in those battles—against both the Germans and the Soviets
In the spring of 1940, the Secret Polish Army got wind of the fact that the Germans were building a massive prison complex outside some backwater town in the southern part of the country
That’s when Pilecki volunteered to sneak into Auschwitz
It was a mission so suicidal that he might as well have asked his commander permission to drink a bucket of bleach
mechanisms_or_explanations: The Nazis were still somewhat imperialist virgins (which, when you look at pictures of Hitler’s mustache, isn’t hard to imagine)
That’s when Pilecki volunteered to sneak into Auschwitz

How did you build your own transistor radio out of spare parts and stolen batteries, MacGyver-style, and then successfully transmit plans for an attack on the prison camp to the Secret Polish Army in Warsaw?
How did you create smuggling rings to bring in food, medicine, and clothing for prisoners, saving countless lives and delivering hope to the remotest desert of the human heart?
He said if you can’t liberate the camp, then at least bomb it
When the doctors discharged him, he headed to the bakery, where he proceeded to “work” until 2:00 a.m., when the last batch of bread finished baking
When we zoom out and get perspective, we realize that while heroes like Pilecki save the world, we swat at gnats and complain that the AC isn’t high enough
Because heroism isn’t just bravery or guts or shrewd maneuvering
And this is why, as a culture, we are so desperate for a hero today: not because things are necessarily so bad, but because we’ve lost the clear “Why?” that drove previous generations

He concluded his statement with “I have tried to live my life such that in the hour of my death I would feel joy rather than fear.” And if that’s not the most hardcore thing you’ve ever heard, then I want some of what
If I worked at Starbucks, instead of writing people’s names on their coffee cup, I’d write the following: One day, you and everyone you love will die
critical_qualifiers: But this is not a story of hope
Fucked in proportions and on scales that today, with the comfort of our free Wi-Fi and oversize Snuggie blankets, you and I can hardly imagine
Pilecki and his crew suspected that Auschwitz, a prison the size of a small town, was likely involved in the disappearances and that it might already house thousands of former Polish soldiers
It was a mission so suicidal that he might as well have asked his commander permission to drink a bucket of bleach
Men were literally worked to death, often performing tasks that were useless or meant nothing
The Secret Polish Army received his messages but figured he was exaggerating
Not Nazi Holocaust–level fucked (not even close), but still, pretty fucked nonetheless
These things are common and are often used in unheroic ways

Over the span of four years, more than 1.3 million people would be systematically sorted, enslaved, tortured, and murdered here, and it would all happen in an area slightly larger than Central Park in Manhattan
As a young man, Pilecki had been a decorated officer in the Polish-Soviet War of 1918
In the spring of 1940, the Secret Polish Army got wind of the fact that the Germans were building a massive prison complex outside some backwater town in the southern part of the country
By the summer of 1940, thousands of military officers and leading Polish nationals were disappearing from western Poland
Regardless, by the end of the 1940, Pilecki, the comic book superhero motherfucker, had still somehow set up an espionage operation
In 1943, Pilecki realized that his plans of a mutiny and prison break were never going to happen: The Secret Polish Army wasn’t coming
When the doctors discharged him, he headed to the bakery, where he proceeded to “work” until 2:00 a.m., when the last batch of bread finished baking
The Communists captured Pilecki in 1947, and they didn’t go easy on him
In 1948, they held a show trial and charged Pilecki with everything from falsifying documents and violating curfew to engaging in espionage and treason
Here’s what a lot of people don’t get: the opposite of happiness is not anger or sadness.1 If you’re angry or sad, that means you still give a fuck about something

That means you still have hope.2 No, the opposite of happiness is hopelessness, an endless gray horizon of resignation and indifference.3 It’s the belief that everything is fucked, so why do anything at all?
